chunks: And as for what was narrated: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, all from Ibn Mahbub from al-Abbas ibn al-Walid from al-Walid ibn Sabih from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

In the case of a man who married a free woman and found her to be a slave girl who had concealed her status from him, he (peace be upon him) said: 'If the one who married her to him was not from her masters, then the marriage is invalid.' I asked: 'What should he do with the dowry she took from him?' He said: 'If he finds something from what he gave her, let him take it; and if he finds nothing, then he has nothing against her. And if the one who married her to him was her guardian, he shall reclaim from her guardian what she took from him, and for her masters upon him is one-tenth of the value of her price if she was a virgin, and if she was not a virgin, then half of one-tenth of her value for what he made lawful of her private part.' He said: 'And she observes from him the waiting period of a slave girl.' I said: 'And if she brings forth a child from him?' He said: 'Her children from him are free, if the marriage was without the permission of the masters.'

His saying (peace be upon him) 'Her children from him are free' implies two things: one is that the one who married her had two witnesses testify before him that she was free, in which case her children are free; the second is that her children are free if the father returns their price, and it is incumbent upon him to return their value. And that which indicates the first division is what was narrated:

key_terms.عِدَّةَ الْأَمَةِ: The waiting period of a slave girl

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a marriage if a free woman conceals her slave status?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith elucidates the fiqh of *ikhtilat* (mixing of status) in marriage, specifically addressing the validity and financial consequences when a free woman conceals her slave status. It distinguishes between marriages contracted by non-masters, which are invalid, and those by guardians, while detailing the masters' rights to compensation and the free status of offspring, reflecting the nuanced Shia jurisprudence on social hierarchy and contractual integrity.
